## Convergence of Sequences

A **sequence** $\{x_n\}$ is an ordered list of numbers indexed
by the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (see [[sequences]]). If $x_n\in\mathbb{R}$
then we say that $\{x_n\}$ is a **real sequence**.

An important property of sequences is **convergence**. If a
sequences converges to some particular value then we say that value is the
**limit** and that the sequence is **convergent**. A sequence that is not
convergent is said to be **divergent**.

Informally, a sequence $\{ x_{n} \}$ has a limit $x$ if the elements of a
sequence become arbitrarily close to the limit $x$ **eventually**. Clearly,
this definition is vague and requires us to specify what we mean by *close*
which in turn requires us to specifically define *distance* more concretely
using a [[metric-spaces.qmd|metric]].

:::{.definition data-title="Standard Euclidean Metric (Distance)"}

For real numbers $a,b\in \mathbb{R}$ the **Euclidean metric** is defined by

$$
d(a,b):=\lvert b-a \rvert.
$$

:::

This is a specific type of **metric**, a function generalizing the concept of
distance in sets, studied in [[metric-spaces]]. The most general concept of
distance however is that of **neighborhoods**, which is a concept we study in
[[topology]].

:::{.definition data-title="Euclidean convergence of Real Sequences"}

The real sequence $\{ x_{n} \}\subset \mathbb{R}$ is said to converge to limit
$x \in \mathbb{R}$, written $x_n\to x$ or $\lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=x$, if for all
$\epsilon>0$ we can find $N$ such that for all $n \geq N$ we have
$\lvert x_{n}-x \rvert<\epsilon$. More succinctly, we write
$$
\forall \epsilon>0,\ \exists N\in\mathbb{N} : \forall n \geq N,\ \lvert x_{n}-x \rvert <\epsilon.
$$

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Sequence Convergence (Metric Spaces)"}

More generally, a sequence $\{x_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in a
[[metric-spaces|metric space]] $(X,d)$ is **convergent** if there exists a
**limit point** $x\in X$ such that
$$
\forall\epsilon>0,\ \exists N\in\mathbb{N},\ \forall n\geq N:\ d(x_n,x)<\epsilon.
$$

:::

**Proof template** for showing $x_n\to x$:

- Let $\epsilon>0$ be arbitrary.
- Solve the inequality $|x_{n}-x|<\epsilon$ to determine how to choose
  $N \in \mathbb{N}$ so that it holds for all $n \geq N$.
- Show that the $N$ found actually works, namely for all $n \geq N$.

:::{.example}

Define real sequence $\{ x_{n} \}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ by
$x_{n}=\frac{1}{n}$. We show that this sequence converges to $x=0$ as
$n \to \infty$. Consider arbitrary $\epsilon>0$. We wish to find $N$ such that
for all $n\geq N$

$$
\left\lvert  \frac{1}{n}  -0\right\rvert <\epsilon \impliedby \frac{1}{n}<\epsilon \impliedby n> \frac{1}{\epsilon}.
$$

Thus we can select $N=\lceil \frac{1}{\epsilon} \rceil+1$ and the proof is
complete.

:::

If a sequence $\{ x_{n} \}$ becomes arbitrarily large as $n \to \infty$ we
write $\lim_{ n \to \infty }x_{n}=\infty$ and say that the sequence
**diverges** or equivalently, **converges to infinity**. Similarly if
$\{  x_{n} \}$ becomes arbitrarily negatively large as $n \to \infty$ we write
$\lim_{ n \to \infty }x_{n}=-\infty$ and say again that the sequence
**diverges** of equivalently, **converges to negative infinity**.

## Sequence Limit Results

:::{.theorem data-title="Limit Uniqueness"}

The limit $\lim_{ n \to \infty }x_{n}=x$ of a real sequence $\{ x_{n} \}$ is
unique.

:::

:::{.proof}
Assume $x^{(1)}, x^{(2)}\in\mathbb{R}$ are both limits of $\{ x_{n} \}$ and let
$\epsilon>0$. There exist $N_1,N_2$ such that
$\lvert x_n-x^{(1)}\rvert<\epsilon/2$ for all $n\geq N_1$ and
$\lvert x_n-x^{(2)}\rvert<\epsilon/2$ for all $n\geq N_2$. For
$n\geq\max(N_1,N_2)$ the triangle inequality gives
$$
\lvert x^{(1)}-x^{(2)}\rvert\leq\lvert x^{(1)}-x_n\rvert+\lvert x_n-x^{(2)}\rvert<\epsilon.
$$
Since $\epsilon>0$ is arbitrary, $x^{(1)}=x^{(2)}$.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Boundedness of Convergent Sequences"}

Every convergent sequence is bounded.

:::

:::{.proof}
Assume $x_{n}\to x$ and take $\epsilon=1$, so there is $N$ with
$\lvert x_{n}-x\rvert<1$ for all $n\geq N$. By the triangle inequality, for
$n\geq N$,
$$
\lvert x_{n}\rvert= \lvert x_{n}-x+x\rvert\leq\lvert x_{n}-x\rvert+\lvert x\rvert< 1 +\lvert x\rvert.
$$
Hence $\lvert x_n\rvert\leq M$ for all $n$, where
$M=\max(\lvert x_{1}\rvert, \dots, \lvert x_{N-1}\rvert, \lvert x\rvert+1)$.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Reciprocal Sequence Convergence"}

Assume that $x_{n}\to x$ where $x_{n}\neq 0$ for all $n$ and $x\neq 0$. Then:

1. For every $\beta>1$ there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that
   $n>N\implies\lvert x_{n}\rvert\geq \frac{\lvert x\rvert}{\beta}$;
2. $\lim_{ n \to \infty }\frac{1}{x_{n}}= \frac{1}{x}$.

:::

:::{.proof}
(1) Let $\epsilon = \frac{(\beta-1)\lvert x\rvert}{\beta}>0$. Since $x_{n}\to x$
there is $N$ such that $\lvert x_{n}-x\rvert<\epsilon$ for all $n>N$. As
$\lvert x\rvert-\lvert x_{n}\rvert\leq \lvert x_{n}-x\rvert$, we get
$$
\lvert x_n\rvert>\lvert x\rvert-\frac{(\beta-1)\lvert x\rvert}{\beta}=\frac{\lvert x\rvert}{\beta}.
$$
(2) Let $\epsilon>0$. By (1) with $\beta=2$ there is $N_{1}$ with
$\frac{1}{\lvert x_{n}\rvert}<\frac{2}{\lvert x\rvert}$ for $n>N_1$, and there is
$N_{2}$ with $\lvert x_{n}-x\rvert<\frac{\lvert x\rvert^2\epsilon}{2}$ for
$n>N_{2}$. For $n>\max(N_{1},N_{2})$,
$$
\left\lvert \frac{1}{x_{n}}- \frac{1}{x}\right\rvert=\frac{\lvert x_{n}-x\rvert}{\lvert x\rvert\lvert x_{n}\rvert}<\frac{2\lvert x_{n}-x\rvert}{\lvert x\rvert^2}<\epsilon.
$$
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Real Sequence Limit Results (Algebraic Limit Theorem)"}

Let $\{ a_{n} \}$ and $\{ b_{n} \}$ be convergent real sequences. Then the
following limits exist:

1. $\lim_{ n \to \infty }(a_{n}\pm b_{n})=\lim_{ n \to \infty }a_{n}\pm \lim_{ n \to \infty }b_{n}$,

2. $\lim_{ n \to \infty }ca_{n}=c\lim_{ n \to \infty }a_{n}$ for all
   $c\in \mathbb{R}$,

3. $\lim_{ n \to \infty }(a_{n}b_{n})=\left(\lim_{ n \to \infty }a_{n}\right)\left(\lim_{ n \to \infty }b_{n}\right)$,

4. $\lim_{ n \to \infty } \frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}= \frac{{\lim_{ n \to \infty }a_{n}}}{\lim_{ n \to \infty }b_{n}}$
   given that $\lim_{ n \to \infty }b_{n}\neq 0$ and $b_n\neq0$ for all $n$, and

5. $\lim_{ n \to \infty }a_{n}^p=(\lim_{ n \to \infty }a_{n})^p$ for all $p>0$
   and $a_{n}>0$.

:::

:::{.proof}
Let $a_n\to a$ and $b_n\to b$. (1) Given $\epsilon>0$ choose $N$ so that
$\lvert a_n-a\rvert,\lvert b_n-b\rvert<\epsilon/2$ for $n\geq N$; then
$\lvert (a_n\pm b_n)-(a\pm b)\rvert<\epsilon$. (2) Follows from (3) with the
constant sequence $b_n=c$. (3) We have
$$
\lvert a_nb_n-ab\rvert\leq\lvert a_n\rvert\lvert b_n-b\rvert+\lvert b\rvert\lvert a_n-a\rvert\leq M\lvert b_n-b\rvert+\lvert b\rvert\lvert a_n-a\rvert,
$$
where $M$ bounds $\{a_n\}$ by the boundedness theorem, and both terms are made
less than $\epsilon/2$ for $n$ large. (4) By the reciprocal theorem
$1/b_n\to1/b$, so apply (3) to $a_n\cdot\frac{1}{b_n}$. (5) is left as an
exercise.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Dominated Sequences"}

For dominated sequence $x_{n}\leq y_{n}$ for all $n>N$ then
$\lim_{ n \to \infty }x_{n}\leq \lim_{ n \to \infty }y_{n}$.

:::

*PROOF:*

:::{.theorem data-title="Squeeze Theorem"}

For some sequence $\{ z_{n} \}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that
$x_{n}\leq z_{n}\leq y_{n}$ for all $n>N$ and
$\lim_{ n \to \infty }x_{n}=\lim_{ n \to \infty }y_{n}=z$ then $\{ z_{n} \}$ is
convergent and
$$
\lim_{ n \to \infty } z_{n}=z.
$$

:::

*PROOF:*

:::{.theorem data-title="Limits of Bounded Monotonic Sequences"}

If a sequence is bounded and monotonic then it is convergent.

:::

*PROOF:*

:::{.theorem data-title="Convergence from Subsequences"}

A sequence is convergent if and only if all of its subsequences are convergent.

:::

*PROOF:*

## Cauchy Convergence

When there is no good candidate for the limit, convergence can be shown using
only information on pairs of terms: a real sequence converges if and only if it
is Cauchy. See [[cauchy-sequence]]. For the limit superior and limit inferior of
a sequence, which exist for every sequence, see [[limsup-liminf]].

## Rate of Convergence

The **asymptotic error** is a measure of the **rate of convergence** of a
sequence. Specifically, given a sequence $\{ x_{n} \}$ we are able to compute
the asymptotic error constant $\lambda$ which provides information on the
differences between the terms of the sequence and the sequence limit $x$.

:::{.definition data-title="Asymptotic Error Constant"}

 If the limit exists and is finite then we can compute the **asymptotic error
 constant** $\lambda$ as
$$
\lambda=\lim_{ n \to \infty } \frac{{\lVert x_{n+1}-x \rVert }}{\lVert x_{n}-x \rVert ^p},
$$
where $p$ is the **order of convergence**.

:::

When $p=1$ we say that the order of convergence is **linear**, when $p=2$ it is
**quadratic**, $p=3$ cubic etc. More generally when $0<p<1$ we say it is
**sublinear** and when $1<p<2$ we say it is **superlinear**. Intuitively, the
order tells you the polynomial rate at which the errors shrink.

**Example:** Consider the sequences $\{ x_{n} \}$ and $\{ y_{n} \}$ defined by
$$
x_{n}=5+\frac{1}{2^n}\quad \&\quad y_{n}=5+\frac{1}{2^{2^n-1}}.
$$
Both converge to $5$. For $x_n$ with $p=1$,
$$
\lambda_{x}=\lim_{ n \to \infty } \frac{2^{-(n+1)}}{2^{-n}} = \frac{1}{2},
$$
so the order is linear. For $y_{n}$ with $p=2$,
$$
\lambda_{y}=\lim_{ n \to \infty } \frac{2^{-(2^{n+1}-1)}}{\left(2^{-(2^{n}-1)}\right)^2}=\frac{2^{-2^{n+1}+1}}{2^{-2^{n+1}+2}}=\frac{1}{2},
$$
so the order is quadratic.
